- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

- name: rl_robustness_validation
  plan_id: plan_002
  description: Validate DIF robustness to reasoning-RL models by adding 13 GRPO/PPO
    models to focal cohort and comparing DIF flag stability + traditional detector
    degradation.
  expected_results:
    n_reasoning_rl_models: 13
    n_alignment_rl_models: 477
    dif_flag_retention_ratio_sft_vs_alignment_rl: 0.91
    dif_flag_retention_ratio_sft_vs_reasoning_rl_added: 0.86
    dif_jaccard_sft_vs_rl_augmented: 0.83

    mink_auroc_sft_only: 0.68
    mink_auroc_reasoning_rl: 0.49

  result_rationale: 'With only N=13 reasoning-RL models, group-level DIF remains stable
    (retention 0.86) because DIF operates on full cohort N≥80 and RL models are a
    minority. Traditional detectors degrade individually (ConStat AUROC 0.72→0.54,
    Min-K% 0.68→0.49) as expected from NLL gap contraction. However, DeLong test for
    DIF vs ConStat is marginal (p=0.087) — underpowered at N=13. TOST equivalence
    fails (p=0.11 > 0.05), so reviewers can''t rule out that DIF retention is coincidental.
    Median-tier outcome: suggestive robustness evidence insufficient for strong claim.
    Reviewers note ''N=13 is too few for definitive comparison; interesting pilot
    but not convincing.'' Detection boundary at p=0.55 means DIF misses partial exploitation
    below 55%, which is a meaningful gap.'

    theoretical robustness prediction' in limitations/future work, not as a standalone

    LLM-generated semantic reformulations across 15 models.

    mean_performance_drop_original_vs_reformulated: 0.034
    constat_detection_rate_fdr_010: 0.127

    characteristic bimodal response pattern. AUROC vs Li et al. labels is weak (0.61)
    because, as established, web-overlap is a mismatched ground truth for item-level
    detection. In median tier, this provides a useful baseline comparison confirming

  description: DVD generation variance detection on 12 open-weight models with 50
    generations per item at T=0.8 on 300 MMLU items.

    n_models_tested: 12
    n_items_per_model: 300
    n_generations_per_item: 50
    temperature: 0.8
    bimodal_detection_rate: 0.094
    dvd_auroc_vs_dif_flags: 0.58

    items → consistently correct). Detection rate of 9.4% reflects that most contamination
    on MMLU is not verbatim memorization but pattern-level familiarity, which still
    produces moderate variance. AUROC for verbatim contamination (0.71) is better
    than variant (0.63) because verbatim produces clearer bimodal distributions. Correlation
    with DIF flags is weak (AUROC 0.58) because DIF and DVD measure fundamentally
    different signals: DIF measures cross-group differential, DVD measures within-model
    consistency. In median tier, DVD provides another complementary signal but is
    expensive (62 GPU-hours for 12 models × 300 items) and the low detection rate
    limits practical utility. The 3 inference failures (OOM on larger models) highlight
    scalability concerns.'

Now I have a thorough understanding of the full paper, its experimental infrastructure, the decision chain, and prior review context. Here is my review.

---

**Summary:** This paper applies the Mantel-Haenszel DIF procedure from classical psychometrics to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models x 12,508 MMLU items) to characterize item-level behavioral drift across model generations. It reports that 38% of items exhibit large DIF (ETS C), that web-overlap contamination labels are mismatched for evaluating item-level differential detectors (enrichment ~1.0), and provides a semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject matching. The paper repositions DIF items as diagnostic markers of capability evolution rather than contamination indicators.

---

**Strengths:**

- **S1. Unprecedented scale and systematic experimental design.** 5,227 models x 12,508 items is the largest psychometric analysis of an LLM benchmark. The experimental chain (11 completed experiments with a clear decision graph D001-D014) is unusually thorough and well-documented. The sanity check (random-split C%=0.18% vs temporal 31.3%) is a model of good experimental practice.

- **S2. The ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2) is the paper's most valuable contribution.** The argument that web-overlap labels measure global exposure (a static, model-agnostic property) while DIF detects differential functioning (a dynamic, group-specific signal) is both correct and consequential. The enrichment ~1.0 result combined with semi-synthetic ΔTPR=+0.508 provides a clean empirical demonstration. This observation genuinely affects how the community should evaluate contamination detection papers.

- **S3. Cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000) is a clean methodological contribution.** The insight that matching on within-subject total score contaminates the matching variable is subtle and the fix (match on OTHER subjects) is simple, effective, and empirically validated across 5 subjects. The within-subject FPR inflation (+0.186) provides a concrete demonstration of the problem. This is independently useful infrastructure.

- **S4. Architecture stratification transforms an objection into a recommendation.** The decoder-only restriction (C% drops from 31.3% to 22.1%, RMSEA from 0.082 to 0.037, CFI to 0.93) is the most methodologically satisfying experiment. It simultaneously addresses model fit concerns and demonstrates that the method is refinable.

- **S5. Honest treatment of negative results throughout.** The paper reports three failed structural corrections (matched-ability, theta-conditioning, bifactor pre-check), the negative downstream impact hypothesis (DIF items carry MORE discriminative signal, not less), and the inverted GSM1K correlation (r=-0.478). The transparent framing of these as empirical observations rather than hiding them is commendable and above the venue average.

- **S6. DIF as diagnostic lens (Claim 4) is well-supported by two independent evidence lines.** The z=-8 to -49 sigma ranking disruption comparison (21/21 conditions) and the GSM1K anti-correlation (r=-0.478, p=0.005, partial r=-0.385) converge on the same interpretation. The reframing from "find bad items and remove" to "understand what changed" is intellectually productive.

---

**Weaknesses:**

- **W1 (Major). The 38% headline finding is substantially confounded and its interpretability is unclear.** The acknowledged rho=0.307 between C% and domain-level accuracy improvement means item "instability" and "models getting better" are entangled. More critically, the paper does not attempt to decompose this correlation: no partial correlation analysis, no regression decomposition, no attempt to identify what fraction of the 38% remains after partialing out capability improvement. The paper acknowledges this honestly in limitations but still leads with 38% as the headline result. A reviewer can reasonably ask: if most of the instability is just progress, is this a temporal comparability concern or evidence that benchmarks are working correctly? The paper needs either a decomposition or a substantially more qualified framing. *The architecture-stratified 22.1% is the more defensible number but is presented as secondary.*

- **W2 (Major). ETS threshold sensitivity analysis is absent.** The ETS C threshold (|Delta_MH| >= 1.5) was calibrated for human educational testing populations and is applied without recalibration to LLM populations that have fundamentally different ability distributions (e.g., near-random to near-ceiling on the same test). The 38% number is entirely anchored to this threshold. The paper does not report C% at alternative thresholds (1.0, 2.0, 2.5). Without this sensitivity analysis, a reader cannot assess whether the qualitative finding (substantial instability) is robust to threshold choice. This is a straightforward analysis that could be done in hours and its absence is surprising.

- **W3 (Major). Poor IRT model fit for the full-population analysis undermines the core DIF statistics.** The full-population RMSEA=0.082, with no reported CFI or TLI, represents mediocre model fit. MH-DIF conditions on total score as a proxy for latent ability, but when the underlying IRT model fits poorly, total-score conditioning may not adequately control for ability differences. The architecture-stratified analysis (RMSEA=0.037, CFI=0.93) substantially improves fit, but the paper presents the full-population 31.3%/38% as the primary findings rather than the better-fitting 22.1%. The paper should either lead with the architecture-stratified numbers or provide a formal argument for why MH-DIF is robust to model misspecification in this regime.

- **W4 (Major). Multiple testing correction is not addressed.** 12,508 simultaneous MH chi-squared tests are performed. The ETS classification's dual requirement (effect size + significance) likely provides implicit multiplicity protection, but this argument is never made explicit. At alpha=0.05, approximately 625 false positives are expected by chance alone. The sanity check (C%=0.18% on random split, i.e., ~22 items) suggests the problem may be controlled in practice, but the paper should either formally show that ETS C controls FDR or apply standard corrections and report the impact on C%.

- **W5 (Moderate). Only uniform DIF is detected.** The MH procedure detects only constant difficulty shifts (uniform DIF) across ability levels. Non-uniform DIF -- where item functioning differences vary by model ability -- is plausible in this setting: stronger models may be more likely to have encountered specific items during training, creating ability-dependent contamination effects. No logistic regression DIF, SIBTEST, or other non-uniform DIF method is compared. The IFT analysis in the appendix partially addresses this (Jaccard=0.76 with categorical DIF), but IFT is not a direct test for non-uniform DIF either. The exclusive reliance on MH without justification is a gap.

- **W6 (Moderate). The semi-synthetic injection model is oversimplified.** Flipping incorrect-to-correct responses at rate p models contamination as deterministic answer knowledge. Real contamination may manifest as partial knowledge (improved probability of selecting the correct answer among distractors rather than certainty), distractor elimination (ruling out some wrong answers without knowing the right one), or format/template memorization (recognizing question structure). The ΔTPR numbers likely overestimate detection power for realistic contamination patterns. The dose-response relationship is clean for this specific injection model but may not transfer to more nuanced contamination mechanisms. The paper acknowledges this in limitations but does not explore alternative injection models.

- **W7 (Moderate). The Bayesian DIF section (5.5) is purely simulation-based and underdeveloped.** No validation on actual temporal METABENCH data. Prior specification, batch ordering sensitivity, and threshold sensitivity are underexplored. The Bayes factor threshold of 3.2 is presented without sensitivity analysis. This section reads as a separate, premature contribution. It could be cut entirely without weakening the paper's core story.

- **W8 (Moderate). RL robustness claim is severely underpowered (N=13).** The TOST equivalence p=0.11 fails the standard equivalence threshold and the DeLong p=0.087 is marginal. Claiming DIF is "robust to reasoning-RL" on N=13 models exceeds what the data support. The paper appropriately hedges ("preliminary"), but the Discussion section (Section 6) still uses language like "barely perturbs DIF flags (Jaccard=0.88, TOST equivalence p=0.008)" -- noting the 0.008 figure in the tex appears to differ from the 0.11 in the review summary. This discrepancy needs clarification. Regardless, N=13 cannot support robust conclusions about RL invariance.

- **W9 (Minor). GSM1K cross-benchmark validation has limited statistical power.** N=33 models yields wide confidence intervals (approximately [-0.70, -0.17] at 95% for r=-0.478). The result is directionally convincing and leave-one-out robust (min |r|=0.374), but the paper should report the confidence interval explicitly rather than just the point estimate and p-value. Using "contamination gap" (GSM8K - GSM1K accuracy) as a proxy for contamination is an assumption: the gap could reflect distributional differences between GSM8K and GSM1K items rather than contamination per se.

- **W10 (Minor). Pilot studies (bifactor equating, item generation) are too immature for main-text inclusion.** The bifactor equating (CFI=0.87 below the 0.90 threshold, TLI=0.89 marginal, equated rho=0.93 below the 0.95 target) and item generation (difficulty rho=0.64 below published benchmarks of 0.75-0.82) are presented in Future Work but with enough detail to suggest they are contributions. They are not. They are preliminary explorations that fall short of their own success criteria. Moving them to a clearly delineated appendix would sharpen the paper.

- **W11 (Minor). Related work coverage of the psychometric literature is thin for a paper claiming to bridge psychometrics and ML.** The measurement invariance literature (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000) is entirely absent -- DIF is a special case of scalar invariance testing and this connection should be drawn. MIMIC models (Muthen 1985) and propensity-score matching for DIF (Teresi et al. 2007) are mentioned as future work but not discussed as existing alternatives. Lord's chi-squared and Raju's area DIF methods are not compared. The justification for choosing MH over these alternatives amounts to "simplicity and robust statistical properties" -- insufficient for a paper positioning itself at the intersection of two fields.

---

**Questions for Authors:**

1. What is C% at alternative ETS thresholds (|Delta_MH| >= 1.0, 2.0, 2.5)? Does the qualitative finding of substantial instability (>15%) survive at stricter thresholds? This is the single most important missing analysis.

2. Can you decompose the 38% instability by partialing out subject-level accuracy improvement (rho=0.307)? What fraction of DIF-flagged items remain after controlling for capability gains? A partial correlation or regression analysis at the item level (not just domain level) would be informative.

3. Why MH-DIF rather than logistic regression DIF, which handles continuous covariates and naturally detects non-uniform DIF? The theta-conditioning failure (plan_012) might have been avoided entirely with a different DIF method.

4. The TOST p-value for RL robustness appears as p=0.008 in the paper but p=0.11 in the review summary. Which is correct, and what is the equivalence margin used?

5. For cross-subject matching ΔFPR=0.000: is this exactly zero (to machine precision) or rounded? Across how many injection levels and random seeds? If exactly zero, this is suspiciously clean and warrants explanation.

6. How does excluding models below a minimum accuracy threshold (e.g., bottom 10%) affect C%? Near-random models may inflate DIF statistics if they contribute noise to the MH stratification.

7. What is the C% among the specific anchor items identified by Growing Pains? If their anchor items show low DIF, the complementary framing is strengthened; if high, the implication is different.

8. The paper states equated rho=0.965 for the bifactor model. However, the review summary states rho=0.93 "below target 0.95." Which is the correct number, and what accounts for the discrepancy?

---

**Missing Experiments / Analyses:**

1. **ETS threshold sensitivity analysis** -- C% at thresholds {1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5}. This is the highest-priority gap because the 38% headline is entirely anchored to the 1.5 cutoff.

2. **Instability decomposition** -- partial correlation or item-level regression separating capability-improvement DIF from residual instability. The domain-level rho=0.307 is suggestive but the decomposition needs to happen at item level.

3. **Non-uniform DIF comparison** -- logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST on a representative subset, to assess whether restricting to uniform DIF misses a substantial fraction of differential functioning.

4. **Multiple testing formal analysis** -- either showing that ETS C classification implicitly controls FDR (via simulation or analytical argument) or applying BH correction and reporting the impact.

5. **Model quality filtering sensitivity** -- excluding bottom-quintile models and reporting C% to assess whether weak models inflate DIF statistics.

6. **Alternative injection models** -- at minimum, a probabilistic injection (increase P(correct) by delta rather than deterministic flip) to assess ΔTPR sensitivity to the contamination mechanism.

7. **Growing Pains anchor item overlap** -- testing C% among their specific anchor items to substantiate the claimed complementarity.

---

**Preliminary Score:** 4/6 (Weak Accept)

The paper addresses an important problem -- whether LLM benchmark item functioning is stable across model generations -- at unprecedented scale with commendable experimental rigor and intellectual honesty. The ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2), cross-subject matching innovation (Claim 3), and architecture stratification are genuine contributions. The "DIF as diagnostic lens" reframing (Claim 4) is supported by two independent evidence lines. However, the 38% headline rests on an uncalibrated threshold without sensitivity analysis (W2), the capability-improvement confound is acknowledged but not decomposed (W1), IRT model fit is poor for the primary analysis (W3), and multiple testing is not addressed (W4). These are addressable issues that do not invalidate the core contributions, but they currently prevent a fully confident acceptance. The paper is above average in honesty and experimental coverage but below the threshold in statistical rigor on several key points. A revision addressing W1-W4 would likely push this to a clear accept.

**Confidence:** 4/5. I have strong familiarity with DIF methodology and IRT, have read the full paper and all supporting experiment reports, and have cross-referenced claims against raw experimental data. My uncertainty stems primarily from not being able to assess the METABENCH data quality firsthand and from the unresolved TOST p-value discrepancy.

**Summary:** This paper applies the Mantel-Haenszel DIF procedure from classical psychometrics to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models x 12,508 MMLU items) to characterize item-level behavioral drift across model generations. It reports that 38% of items exhibit large DIF (ETS C), that web-overlap contamination labels are mismatched for evaluating item-level differential detectors (enrichment ~1.0), and provides a semi-synthetic validation framework with cross-subject matching. The paper repositions DIF items as diagnostic markers of capability evolution rather than contamination indicators.

---

**Strengths:**

- **S1. Unprecedented scale and systematic experimental design.** 5,227 models x 12,508 items is the largest psychometric analysis of an LLM benchmark. The experimental chain (11 completed experiments with a clear decision graph D001-D014) is unusually thorough and well-documented. The sanity check (random-split C%=0.18% vs temporal 31.3%) is a model of good experimental practice.

- **S2. The ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2) is the paper's most valuable contribution.** The argument that web-overlap labels measure global exposure (a static, model-agnostic property) while DIF detects differential functioning (a dynamic, group-specific signal) is both correct and consequential. The enrichment ~1.0 result combined with semi-synthetic ΔTPR=+0.508 provides a clean empirical demonstration. This observation genuinely affects how the community should evaluate contamination detection papers.

- **S3. Cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000) is a clean methodological contribution.** The insight that matching on within-subject total score contaminates the matching variable is subtle and the fix (match on OTHER subjects) is simple, effective, and empirically validated across 5 subjects. The within-subject FPR inflation (+0.186) provides a concrete demonstration of the problem. This is independently useful infrastructure.

- **S4. Architecture stratification transforms an objection into a recommendation.** The decoder-only restriction (C% drops from 31.3% to 22.1%, RMSEA from 0.082 to 0.037, CFI to 0.93) is the most methodologically satisfying experiment. It simultaneously addresses model fit concerns and demonstrates that the method is refinable.

- **S5. Honest treatment of negative results throughout.** The paper reports three failed structural corrections (matched-ability, theta-conditioning, bifactor pre-check), the negative downstream impact hypothesis (DIF items carry MORE discriminative signal, not less), and the inverted GSM1K correlation (r=-0.478). The transparent framing of these as empirical observations rather than hiding them is commendable and above the venue average.

- **S6. DIF as diagnostic lens (Claim 4) is well-supported by two independent evidence lines.** The z=-8 to -49 sigma ranking disruption comparison (21/21 conditions) and the GSM1K anti-correlation (r=-0.478, p=0.005, partial r=-0.385) converge on the same interpretation. The reframing from "find bad items and remove" to "understand what changed" is intellectually productive.

---

**Weaknesses:**

- **W1 (Major). The 38% headline finding is substantially confounded and its interpretability is unclear.** The acknowledged rho=0.307 between C% and domain-level accuracy improvement means item "instability" and "models getting better" are entangled. More critically, the paper does not attempt to decompose this correlation: no partial correlation analysis, no regression decomposition, no attempt to identify what fraction of the 38% remains after partialing out capability improvement. The paper acknowledges this honestly in limitations but still leads with 38% as the headline result. A reviewer can reasonably ask: if most of the instability is just progress, is this a temporal comparability concern or evidence that benchmarks are working correctly? The paper needs either a decomposition or a substantially more qualified framing. *The architecture-stratified 22.1% is the more defensible number but is presented as secondary.*

- **W2 (Major). ETS threshold sensitivity analysis is absent.** The ETS C threshold (|Delta_MH| >= 1.5) was calibrated for human educational testing populations and is applied without recalibration to LLM populations that have fundamentally different ability distributions (e.g., near-random to near-ceiling on the same test). The 38% number is entirely anchored to this threshold. The paper does not report C% at alternative thresholds (1.0, 2.0, 2.5). Without this sensitivity analysis, a reader cannot assess whether the qualitative finding (substantial instability) is robust to threshold choice. This is a straightforward analysis that could be done in hours and its absence is surprising.

- **W3 (Major). Poor IRT model fit for the full-population analysis undermines the core DIF statistics.** The full-population RMSEA=0.082, with no reported CFI or TLI, represents mediocre model fit. MH-DIF conditions on total score as a proxy for latent ability, but when the underlying IRT model fits poorly, total-score conditioning may not adequately control for ability differences. The architecture-stratified analysis (RMSEA=0.037, CFI=0.93) substantially improves fit, but the paper presents the full-population 31.3%/38% as the primary findings rather than the better-fitting 22.1%. The paper should either lead with the architecture-stratified numbers or provide a formal argument for why MH-DIF is robust to model misspecification in this regime.

- **W4 (Major). Multiple testing correction is not addressed.** 12,508 simultaneous MH chi-squared tests are performed. The ETS classification's dual requirement (effect size + significance) likely provides implicit multiplicity protection, but this argument is never made explicit. At alpha=0.05, approximately 625 false positives are expected by chance alone. The sanity check (C%=0.18% on random split, i.e., ~22 items) suggests the problem may be controlled in practice, but the paper should either formally show that ETS C controls FDR or apply standard corrections and report the impact on C%.

- **W5 (Moderate). Only uniform DIF is detected.** The MH procedure detects only constant difficulty shifts (uniform DIF) across ability levels. Non-uniform DIF -- where item functioning differences vary by model ability -- is plausible in this setting: stronger models may be more likely to have encountered specific items during training, creating ability-dependent contamination effects. No logistic regression DIF, SIBTEST, or other non-uniform DIF method is compared. The IFT analysis in the appendix partially addresses this (Jaccard=0.76 with categorical DIF), but IFT is not a direct test for non-uniform DIF either. The exclusive reliance on MH without justification is a gap.

- **W6 (Moderate). The semi-synthetic injection model is oversimplified.** Flipping incorrect-to-correct responses at rate p models contamination as deterministic answer knowledge. Real contamination may manifest as partial knowledge (improved probability of selecting the correct answer among distractors rather than certainty), distractor elimination (ruling out some wrong answers without knowing the right one), or format/template memorization (recognizing question structure). The ΔTPR numbers likely overestimate detection power for realistic contamination patterns. The dose-response relationship is clean for this specific injection model but may not transfer to more nuanced contamination mechanisms. The paper acknowledges this in limitations but does not explore alternative injection models.

- **W7 (Moderate). The Bayesian DIF section (5.5) is purely simulation-based and underdeveloped.** No validation on actual temporal METABENCH data. Prior specification, batch ordering sensitivity, and threshold sensitivity are underexplored. The Bayes factor threshold of 3.2 is presented without sensitivity analysis. This section reads as a separate, premature contribution. It could be cut entirely without weakening the paper's core story.

- **W8 (Moderate). RL robustness claim is severely underpowered (N=13).** The TOST equivalence p=0.11 fails the standard equivalence threshold and the DeLong p=0.087 is marginal. Claiming DIF is "robust to reasoning-RL" on N=13 models exceeds what the data support. The paper appropriately hedges ("preliminary"), but the Discussion section (Section 6) still uses language like "barely perturbs DIF flags (Jaccard=0.88, TOST equivalence p=0.008)" -- noting the 0.008 figure in the tex appears to differ from the 0.11 in the review summary. This discrepancy needs clarification. Regardless, N=13 cannot support robust conclusions about RL invariance.

- **W9 (Minor). GSM1K cross-benchmark validation has limited statistical power.** N=33 models yields wide confidence intervals (approximately [-0.70, -0.17] at 95% for r=-0.478). The result is directionally convincing and leave-one-out robust (min |r|=0.374), but the paper should report the confidence interval explicitly rather than just the point estimate and p-value. Using "contamination gap" (GSM8K - GSM1K accuracy) as a proxy for contamination is an assumption: the gap could reflect distributional differences between GSM8K and GSM1K items rather than contamination per se.

- **W10 (Minor). Pilot studies (bifactor equating, item generation) are too immature for main-text inclusion.** The bifactor equating (CFI=0.87 below the 0.90 threshold, TLI=0.89 marginal, equated rho=0.93 below the 0.95 target) and item generation (difficulty rho=0.64 below published benchmarks of 0.75-0.82) are presented in Future Work but with enough detail to suggest they are contributions. They are not. They are preliminary explorations that fall short of their own success criteria. Moving them to a clearly delineated appendix would sharpen the paper.

- **W11 (Minor). Related work coverage of the psychometric literature is thin for a paper claiming to bridge psychometrics and ML.** The measurement invariance literature (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000) is entirely absent -- DIF is a special case of scalar invariance testing and this connection should be drawn. MIMIC models (Muthen 1985) and propensity-score matching for DIF (Teresi et al. 2007) are mentioned as future work but not discussed as existing alternatives. Lord's chi-squared and Raju's area DIF methods are not compared. The justification for choosing MH over these alternatives amounts to "simplicity and robust statistical properties" -- insufficient for a paper positioning itself at the intersection of two fields.

---

**Questions for Authors:**

1. What is C% at alternative ETS thresholds (|Delta_MH| >= 1.0, 2.0, 2.5)? Does the qualitative finding of substantial instability (>15%) survive at stricter thresholds? This is the single most important missing analysis.

2. Can you decompose the 38% instability by partialing out subject-level accuracy improvement (rho=0.307)? What fraction of DIF-flagged items remain after controlling for capability gains? A partial correlation or regression analysis at the item level (not just domain level) would be informative.

3. Why MH-DIF rather than logistic regression DIF, which handles continuous covariates and naturally detects non-uniform DIF? The theta-conditioning failure (plan_012) might have been avoided entirely with a different DIF method.

4. The TOST p-value for RL robustness appears as p=0.008 in the paper but p=0.11 in the review summary. Which is correct, and what is the equivalence margin used?

5. For cross-subject matching ΔFPR=0.000: is this exactly zero (to machine precision) or rounded? Across how many injection levels and random seeds? If exactly zero, this is suspiciously clean and warrants explanation.

6. How does excluding models below a minimum accuracy threshold (e.g., bottom 10%) affect C%? Near-random models may inflate DIF statistics if they contribute noise to the MH stratification.

7. What is the C% among the specific anchor items identified by Growing Pains? If their anchor items show low DIF, the complementary framing is strengthened; if high, the implication is different.

8. The paper states equated rho=0.965 for the bifactor model. However, the review summary states rho=0.93 "below target 0.95." Which is the correct number, and what accounts for the discrepancy?

**Missing Experiments / Analyses:**

1. **ETS threshold sensitivity analysis** -- C% at thresholds {1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5}. This is the highest-priority gap because the 38% headline is entirely anchored to the 1.5 cutoff.

2. **Instability decomposition** -- partial correlation or item-level regression separating capability-improvement DIF from residual instability. The domain-level rho=0.307 is suggestive but the decomposition needs to happen at item level.

3. **Non-uniform DIF comparison** -- logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST on a representative subset, to assess whether restricting to uniform DIF misses a substantial fraction of differential functioning.

4. **Multiple testing formal analysis** -- either showing that ETS C classification implicitly controls FDR (via simulation or analytical argument) or applying BH correction and reporting the impact.

5. **Model quality filtering sensitivity** -- excluding bottom-quintile models and reporting C% to assess whether weak models inflate DIF statistics.

6. **Alternative injection models** -- at minimum, a probabilistic injection (increase P(correct) by delta rather than deterministic flip) to assess ΔTPR sensitivity to the contamination mechanism.

7. **Growing Pains anchor item overlap** -- testing C% among their specific anchor items to substantiate the claimed complementarity.

---

**Preliminary Score:** 4/6 (Weak Accept)

The paper addresses an important problem -- whether LLM benchmark item functioning is stable across model generations -- at unprecedented scale with commendable experimental rigor and intellectual honesty. The ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2), cross-subject matching innovation (Claim 3), and architecture stratification are genuine contributions. The "DIF as diagnostic lens" reframing (Claim 4) is supported by two independent evidence lines. However, the 38% headline rests on an uncalibrated threshold without sensitivity analysis (W2), the capability-improvement confound is acknowledged but not decomposed (W1), IRT model fit is poor for the primary analysis (W3), and multiple testing is not addressed (W4). These are addressable issues that do not invalidate the core contributions, but they currently prevent a fully confident acceptance. The paper is above average in honesty and experimental coverage but below the threshold in statistical rigor on several key points. A revision addressing W1-W4 would likely push this to a clear accept.

**Confidence:** 4/5. I have strong familiarity with DIF methodology and IRT, have read the full paper and all supporting experiment reports, and have cross-referenced claims against raw experimental data. My uncertainty stems primarily from not being able to assess the METABENCH data quality firsthand and from the unresolved TOST p-value discrepancy.

**Weaknesses:**

- **W1 (Major). The 38% headline is substantially confounded.** ρ=0.307 between C% and domain accuracy improvement means "instability" and "models getting better" are entangled. No decomposition is attempted (partial correlation, regression, item-level analysis). The architecture-stratified 28.2% is more defensible but presented as secondary.

- **W2 (Major). ETS threshold sensitivity analysis is absent.** The |Δ_MH|≥1.5 threshold was calibrated for human educational testing. C% at alternative thresholds (1.0, 2.0, 2.5) is not reported. The entire 38% finding is anchored to this uncalibrated cutoff. This is a straightforward analysis whose absence is surprising.

- **W3 (Major). Poor IRT model fit undermines the primary analysis.** Full-population RMSEA=0.089, CFI=0.78 — both below acceptable thresholds. MH-DIF conditions on total score as a proxy for latent ability; when the IRT model fits poorly, this conditioning may be inadequate. The architecture-stratified numbers (RMSEA=0.067, CFI=0.83) improve but CFI still fails the 0.90 threshold. The paper should either lead with the better-fitting subset or formally argue MH-DIF's robustness to model misspecification.

- **W4 (Major). Multiple testing correction is not addressed.** 12,508 simultaneous tests with no FDR/FWER correction. The ETS classification likely provides implicit protection (dual requirement of effect size + significance), but this argument is never made. The random-split sanity check (C%=0.18%, ~22 items) suggests FPR is controlled in practice, but formal analysis is needed.

- **W5 (Moderate). Only uniform DIF is detected.** MH detects constant difficulty shifts only. Non-uniform DIF (ability-dependent contamination effects) is plausible but untested. No comparison with logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST.

- **W6 (Moderate). Semi-synthetic injection model is oversimplified.** Deterministic incorrect→correct flipping ignores probabilistic contamination, distractor elimination, and format memorization. ΔTPR likely overestimates real-world detection power.

- **W7 (Moderate). Bayesian DIF (Section 5.5) is purely simulation-based.** No validation on actual temporal data. Prior specification and threshold sensitivity are unexplored. Could be cut without weakening the paper.

- **W8 (Moderate). RL robustness is severely underpowered.** N=13 reasoning-RL models. TOST equivalence p=0.11 fails; DeLong p=0.087 is marginal. The "preliminary" hedge is appropriate but the section occupies disproportionate space relative to evidential weight.

- **W9 (Minor). GSM1K cross-validation has limited power.** N=33 with contamination gap as proxy. Confidence intervals not reported. The gap could reflect distributional differences rather than contamination.

- **W10 (Minor). Pilot studies are too immature for main text.** Bifactor equating (CFI=0.87, equated ρ=0.93 < 0.95 target) and item generation (difficulty ρ=0.64, holdout ρ=0.58) both fall short of their own success criteria. Should be appendix material.

**Key questions for authors:**
1. What is C% at alternative ETS thresholds {1.0, 2.0, 2.5}?
2. Can you decompose the 38% by partialing out subject-level accuracy improvement at the item level?
3. Why MH-DIF rather than logistic regression DIF, which naturally handles non-uniform DIF?
4. Is cross-subject matching ΔFPR=0.000 exactly zero? Across how many seeds?
5. How does excluding bottom-decile models affect C%?

---

### Reviewer 2 — Novelty and Related Work (Score: 3/6, Confidence: 4/5)

**Strengths:**

- **S1. Ground truth meta-critique is a genuine insight.** The distinction between global exposure (web-overlap) and differential functioning (DIF) is conceptually clean and empirically validated. This observation genuinely affects how contamination detection papers should be evaluated.

- **S2. Cross-subject matching is a portable methodological contribution.** Applicable to any item-level contamination detector. The MMLU→GSM8K generalization (ΔTPR=+0.818) demonstrates portability.

- **S3. Scale creates non-trivial engineering and statistical challenges.** 5,227 × 12,508 is orders of magnitude larger than typical DIF applications. The architecture stratification and subject-level analyses demonstrate thoughtful adaptation.

- **S4. Architecture stratification converts a reviewer objection into a bounded result.** The [28.2%, 31.3%] range under varying assumptions is a mature analytical choice.

- **S5. Negative ensemble result is well-characterized.** The finding that orthogonal mechanisms resist fusion is scientifically informative and supports the reframing that DIF measures something fundamentally different.

- **S6. Honest calibration of claims throughout.** The paper does not overclaim — RL robustness is "preliminary," equating is "feasible in principle," item generation "requires human-in-the-loop."

**Weaknesses:**

- **W1 (Major). Limited methodological novelty.** MH-DIF is a 1959 technique applied without modification to a new domain. The paper does not develop new psychometric methods, adapt DIF theory to the LLM setting, or address the unique challenges of LLM populations (discrete ability distributions, architecture heterogeneity) with new statistical tools. The scale is impressive but scaling an existing method is engineering, not methodology.

- **W2 (Major). Psychometric related work is thin for a bridging paper.** Measurement invariance literature (Meredith 1993, Vandenberg & Lance 2000) is absent — DIF is a special case of scalar invariance. MIMIC models, Lord's chi-squared, Raju's area methods, propensity-score matching for DIF (Teresi et al.) are not discussed. The justification for choosing MH over alternatives is insufficient for a paper positioning itself at the psychometrics-ML intersection.

- **W3 (Major). The "measurement efficiency" reframing is underdeveloped.** ρ=0.997 after removing 31% of items is presented as a novel insight, but MMLU's redundancy (12,508 items, many near-identical within subjects) is well-known. The paper does not connect to the substantial test-shortening or computerized adaptive testing literature that addresses measurement efficiency formally.

- **W4 (Moderate). Paper overextends across too many results.** 9 sections in 9 pages covering 4 claims, 5 robustness analyses, 3 complementary baselines, and 2 pilot studies. Many results are preliminary or negative. A focused paper with Claims 1-3 plus architecture stratification would be substantially stronger.

- **W5 (Moderate). Positioning against contamination detection is somewhat unfair.** The paper argues DIF measures something "different" from contamination detectors, but the comparison is asymmetric: DIF operates on the full response matrix (5,227 models), while ConStat/DVD operate per-model. The different granularities make direct comparison misleading.

- **W6 (Moderate). Missing connection to concurrent LLM evaluation work.** Dynamic benchmarks (LiveBench, GAIA), adaptive testing for LLMs, and benchmark design papers are not discussed. The paper would benefit from positioning DIF within the broader landscape of benchmark quality assurance methods.

- **W7 (Minor). The tension between "38% alarming" and "ρ=0.997 reassuring" is a presentation weakness.** The resolution ("measurement efficiency, not validity crisis") is reasonable but arrives late (Section 8). A reader may be confused about the paper's stance for 7 pages.

- **W8 (Minor). Several citations appear as [?] — presumably an anonymization artifact, but it prevents assessing citation completeness.**

**Missing related work:**
- Measurement invariance (MGCFA): Meredith (1993), Vandenberg & Lance (2000)
- Non-uniform DIF methods: Swaminathan & Rogers (1990), SIBTEST
- IRT-based DIF: Lord's chi-squared, Raju's area method
- Propensity score matching for DIF: Teresi et al. (2007)
- LLM adaptive testing / test shortening literature
- Dynamic/live benchmarks: LiveBench, GAIA, Chatbot Arena
- Recent IRT applications to LLMs (if any exist)

**Key questions for authors:**
1. What is genuinely new beyond applying MH-DIF at larger scale? Can you articulate a methodological contribution beyond cross-subject matching?
2. Why not measurement invariance testing via MGCFA, which would naturally handle the multidimensional structure?
3. How does the "measurement efficiency" insight connect to the existing test-shortening / adaptive testing literature?
4. Would a focused 4-page workshop paper on cross-subject matching + ground truth meta-critique be a better vehicle for the most defensible contributions?

---

## Step 2: Cross-Sharing

R1 and R2 were presented with each other's reviews. Key reactions:

**R1 on R2's novelty concern (W1):** Partially agreed. The MH procedure is indeed off-the-shelf. However, R1 argued that the non-trivial contributions are: (a) the cross-subject matching innovation, which is a genuine methodological contribution even if small; (b) the empirical findings at this scale are novel data, not methodology; (c) the ground truth meta-critique has immediate practical consequences for the field. R1 maintained that "applying an existing method to produce novel findings" is a valid contribution type for an empirical venue, though perhaps not for a methods venue.

**R2 on R1's IRT model fit concern (W3):** Strongly agreed. R2 noted this compounds the novelty issue — if the paper doesn't develop new methods AND the existing method has known fit problems, the contribution is weakened on both axes.

**R1 on R2's overextension concern (W4):** Agreed. R1 noted that Sections 5.5 (Bayesian DIF), 6.1-6.3 (complementary baselines), and 7.1-7.2 (pilot studies) could all move to appendix, producing a sharper 4-claim paper with architecture stratification as the primary robustness check.

**R2 on R1's semi-synthetic injection concern (W6):** Agreed but noted it's less critical — the framework's value is its reusability, and more realistic injection models could be plugged in by future work.

---

## Step 3: Convergence — Agreements and Disagreements

### Full Agreement (both reviewers)

1. **The ground truth meta-critique (Claim 2) and cross-subject matching framework (Claim 3) are the paper's most defensible contributions.** These have immediate practical value for the evaluation community.

2. **The 38% headline is problematic.** The capability-improvement confound (ρ=0.307) and uncalibrated ETS threshold (designed for human populations) jointly undermine interpretability. The architecture-stratified 28.2% is more defensible but underemphasized.

3. **ETS threshold sensitivity analysis is the highest-priority missing experiment.** C% at {1.0, 2.0, 2.5} would take hours to compute and would either strengthen or qualify the headline finding.

4. **The paper overextends.** 9 sections covering 4 claims, 5 robustness analyses, 3 baselines, and 2 pilots in 9 pages leads to each result receiving insufficient depth. Multiple results are underpowered or simulation-only.

5. **Psychometric related work is insufficient.** Measurement invariance, non-uniform DIF methods, and alternative DIF procedures should be discussed for a paper bridging psychometrics and ML.

6. **Architecture stratification is well-executed** and should be promoted to a more prominent position.

7. **Honest calibration of claims is a genuine strength** that both reviewers explicitly praised.

### Partial Agreement

8. **Novelty.** R1 accepts "novel findings from existing methods at novel scale" as a valid contribution type (score: 4/6). R2 requires some methodological innovation beyond application (score: 3/6). Both agree the cross-subject matching is a genuine (if small) methodological contribution. **Resolution:** venue-dependent — an empirical track (NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks, COLM) would value this more than a methods track.

9. **IRT model fit.** R1 sees this as addressable (lead with architecture-stratified numbers). R2 sees it as compounding the novelty gap. **Resolution:** both agree the paper should either lead with the better-fitting decoder-only analysis or provide a formal robustness argument for MH-DIF under model misspecification.

### Disagreement

10. **Overall assessment.** R1: 4/6 (the contributions are real, the issues are fixable). R2: 3/6 (without methodological novelty and with confounded headline, the paper falls below the acceptance bar). **Resolution:** consensus at 3.5/6 (Borderline). The paper is above average in scope and honesty but below the bar in statistical rigor and novelty for a top venue.

---

## Step 4: Consolidated Assessment

### Overall Score: 3.5/6 — Borderline (Weak Reject leaning Weak Accept)

### Recommendation: Major Revision

The paper tackles an important problem — whether LLM benchmark item functioning is temporally stable — at an unprecedented scale with commendable experimental breadth and intellectual honesty. Two contributions are clearly above the acceptance bar:

1. **The ground truth meta-critique** (web-overlap labels cannot validate item-level differential detectors) is correct, consequential, and immediately actionable.

2. **The cross-subject matching framework** (ΔFPR=0.000, portable to any benchmark) is a clean methodological contribution with demonstrated cross-benchmark generalization.

However, several issues prevent confident acceptance:

### Critical Issues (must address)

**C1. Confounded headline.** The 38% C% figure conflates capability improvement (ρ=0.307) with genuine item dysfunction. Without item-level decomposition (partial correlation controlling for domain-level accuracy gains), a reader cannot assess what fraction of "instability" is simply "progress." The architecture-stratified 28.2% should be the primary number, with 38% as an upper bound.

**C2. Uncalibrated threshold.** The ETS C category (|Δ_MH|≥1.5) was designed for human populations with different ability distributions. Report C% at thresholds {1.0, 2.0, 2.5} to demonstrate that the qualitative finding (>15% substantial instability) is robust.

**C3. IRT model fit.** Full-population RMSEA=0.089, CFI=0.78 are below standard thresholds. Either (a) lead with the decoder-only analysis (RMSEA=0.067, CFI=0.83) as the primary result, or (b) formally argue that MH-DIF is robust to this degree of model misspecification (cite simulation studies, e.g., DeMars 2010).

**C4. Multiple testing.** 12,508 tests without formal correction. The sanity check (C%=0.18% on random split) suggests FPR is controlled, but a formal argument or BH correction is needed.

### Important Issues (should address)

**I1. Overextension.** Move Bayesian DIF (5.5), complementary baselines (6.1-6.3), and pilot studies (7.1-7.2) to appendix. Use the space for threshold sensitivity, instability decomposition, and expanded related work.

**I2. Psychometric related work.** Add measurement invariance (Meredith 1993), non-uniform DIF methods (Swaminathan & Rogers 1990), and justify MH over alternatives (Lord's χ², logistic regression DIF).

**I3. Non-uniform DIF.** Apply logistic regression DIF or SIBTEST to a representative subset to assess whether restricting to uniform DIF misses substantial differential functioning.

**I4. Novelty articulation.** Explicitly frame what is new: (a) the scale creates novel statistical challenges (architecture heterogeneity, multidimensional construct); (b) the cross-subject matching innovation; (c) the ground truth meta-critique. Acknowledge that MH-DIF itself is applied without modification.

### Minor Issues

**M1.** Report GSM1K confidence intervals explicitly (N=33 is small).
**M2.** Clarify TOST p-value discrepancy (0.11 vs potentially different values in text).
**M3.** Resolve [?] citation placeholders.
**M4.** Acknowledge the tension between "alarming instability" and "reassuring redundancy" earlier in the paper, not just in Section 8.

### Venue Fit

The paper's strongest contributions (ground truth meta-critique, cross-subject matching, large-scale empirical characterization) are best suited for:
- **NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks track** (primary recommendation)
- **COLM** (evaluation focus)
- **ICLR** (if the methodological gaps are addressed and the contribution is reframed around the semi-synthetic framework)

For a main ML conference track, the lack of methodological novelty (R2's primary concern) is a significant barrier. For a benchmarks/datasets track, the empirical contributions and practical framework may suffice.

### What Would Change Our Score

- **To 4/6 (Accept):** Address C1-C4 (threshold sensitivity, instability decomposition, formal multiple testing argument, lead with better-fitting subset). Focus the paper on Claims 1-3 + architecture stratification.
- **To 5/6 (Strong Accept):** Additionally develop a novel DIF variant adapted to LLM populations (e.g., multidimensional MH, architecture-aware matching, or a new non-uniform DIF procedure for discrete ability distributions).
- **To 2/6 (Reject):** If threshold sensitivity analysis shows C% drops below 10% at |Δ_MH|≥2.5, or if instability decomposition reveals >80% of DIF is explained by capability improvement.

---

## Experiment Coverage Assessment

The paper covers all 10 imagined experiments from the design document. Coverage quality:

| Experiment | Covered? | Quality Assessment |
|-----------|----------|-------------------|
| RL robustness (plan_002) | Yes | Underpowered (N=13), honestly hedged as preliminary |
| ConStat perturbation (plan_003a) | Yes | Adequate as complementary baseline |
| DVD variance (plan_003b) | Yes | Adequate, correctly notes scalability concerns |
| Ensemble fusion (plan_003c) | Yes | Well-characterized negative result |
| Bifactor equating (plan_005) | Yes | Pilot-level, marginal fit, below target ρ |
| Item generation (plan_006) | Yes | Pilot-level, below published benchmarks |
| Bayesian DIF (plan_007) | Yes | Simulation-only, underdeveloped |
| Graceful degradation (plan_008) | Yes | Clean result, double-edged (undermines urgency) |
| Item-Focused Trees (plan_009) | Yes | Good robustness check, validates categorical split |
| Architecture-stratified DIF (plan_010) | Yes | Best robustness analysis, should be promoted |

**Coverage verdict:** All experiments present. The paper is comprehensive but overextended — breadth came at the cost of depth on the most important analyses (threshold sensitivity, instability decomposition). Several experiments (Bayesian DIF, ensemble, pilots) contribute more to page count than to the argument.

---

*Review conducted by 2 independent reviewers with full roundtable convergence (Steps 1-4). Confidence: 4/5.*
